a: Woe to those going down to Egypt for help
p: Isaiah's last woes still target the treaty with Egypt that Hezekiah's court was making around 703–701 BC.
b: In these years Egypt was ruled by the Cushite (Nubian) kings of the 25th Dynasty, who were glad to back revolts against Assyria in Philistia and Judah. Isaiah had already condemned envoys carrying gifts south on donkeys (30:1–7). Here he speaks to the planners in Jerusalem once more. The Rabshakeh will later use the same argument against Hezekiah, calling Egypt a crushed reed (36:6; see the note on 2 Kings 18:21). The Egyptian army did march out in 701, and Sennacherib says he beat it at Eltekeh. In Isaiah's eyes the alliance was not just bad strategy. It was a choice of whom to trust, made without asking the LORD (30:2).

a: who lean on horses
p: The law of the king had forbidden exactly this: horses brought back from Egypt.
b: Deuteronomy's law for kings says a king "must not get himself many horses, or send the people back to Egypt to get more horses" (Deuteronomy 17:16). Solomon broke it (1 Kings 10:28–29). Egypt was famous for chariot horses, and a small hill state like Judah could not breed enough of its own. Psalm 20:7 sets the two kinds of trust side by side: "These have chariots, and those have horses, / but we call on the name of the LORD our God." Isaiah's verse uses the same contrast. Trust in chariots "because there are many" is the opposite of looking to the Holy One of Israel.

a: Yet he too is wise
p: A dry joke: the king's advisers thought themselves clever, but the LORD is wise too.
b: The planners in Jerusalem prided themselves on their counsel (29:14–15; 30:1). Isaiah answers with understatement: "he too is wise." God's wisdom shows in the fact that "he has not set aside his words": what he said about Egypt will happen. "The house of evildoers" is Judah's war party, and "the ones who help wrongdoers" are the Egyptians. Both fall together in 31:3.
orig: וְגַם־הוּא חָכָם (wegam-hu chakham), 'and also he is wise'

a: their horses are flesh, and not spirit
p: Isaiah sets 'human' against 'God' and 'flesh' against 'spirit': the weakness of creatures against the power of God.
b: Hebrew 'adam (a human being) and basar (flesh) mean what is mortal and weak. 'El (God) and ruach (spirit, wind, breath) mean life and power that come from God (Genesis 6:3). The point is not that Egypt's horses lack a soul. It is that Egypt is a creature, and creatures fail. Jeremiah 17:5 says the same: in the KJV, cursed is the man who "maketh flesh his arm." The Greek translation flattens the second line to "flesh, and there is no help."
orig: אָדָם וְלֹא־אֵל ... בָּשָׂר וְלֹא־רוּחַ ('adam welo-'el ... basar welo-ruach)

a: to wage war on Mount Zion and on its hill
t: Fighting for Zion, or against it?
p: The Hebrew can mean the LORD comes down to fight upon Zion or against it. The lion picture cuts both ways.
b: Litsbo' 'al usually means "to fight against" (29:7–8 uses the same words for the nations attacking Zion). Read that way, the LORD is the lion who will not let go of his prey, Jerusalem, and no human shepherds can scare him off; the promise of rescue in 31:5 then comes as a surprise. Read as "fight on (or for) Mount Zion," as in the KJV, the lion stands guard over what is his, and the "shepherds" are the Assyrian kings. Many recent commentators prefer the first sense, with 31:5 as the turn from judgment to rescue that runs through Isaiah 28–33; others keep the second. Either way, God, not Egypt, decides Zion's fate.

a: pass over it
p: Pasach, 'pass over', is the word of the first Passover, used here for God sparing Jerusalem.
b: Outside Exodus 12, where the LORD "passes over" the houses marked with blood (Exodus 12:13, 23, 27), the verb pasach in this sense appears only here. The four verbs of the verse, guard, rescue, pass over, bring out safe, picture Jerusalem as a new Egypt night in which the destroyer spares God's people. Later Jewish tradition made the link explicit: the Passover poem in the Haggadah counts the night Sennacherib's army fell (37:36) among the wonders done on Passover night.

a: Like birds that fly
p: After a lion, a flock of birds: the LORD hovers over Jerusalem as birds circle their young.
b: The images seem to clash, but both say that no one will take Zion out of the LORD's grip. Birds that dart and scream over a nest to drive off a hawk or a snake are a picture of fierce care. Deuteronomy 32:11 pictures God as an eagle spreading its wings over its young, and Psalm 91:4 speaks of shelter under his wings. Jesus used a gentler form of the picture over the same city: "the way a bird gathers her young under her wings. And you would not" (Matthew 23:37).

a: Return, you Israelites
p: Shuv, 'turn, return', is Isaiah's word for repentance, and the verse slips from 'you' to 'they'.
b: The call is short and urgent. Shuv means to turn around and go back, the root of the name Shear-jashub, "a remnant will return" (7:3; 10:21). The second line speaks of Israel in the third person, "the one they have rebelled against so deeply," as if the prophet turns from his hearers to describe them. "So deeply" (he'emiqu) is the same verb as in 29:15, those who "burrow deep" to hide their plans from the LORD: they went deep in scheming and deep in revolt.

a: his worthless idols of silver and his worthless idols of gold
p: The same day was promised in 2:20, when people will toss their idols out to the moles and the bats.
b: On "that day" of the LORD's action, idols will be seen for what they are. In 2:20 people "will toss / the worthless idols of silver and of gold" to the moles and bats; in 30:22 they throw them away like a soiled cloth. Here the turning away from idols is the fruit of the call to return in 31:6. The last line is pointed: what "your own hands made for you" was a sin, not a god. Hezekiah's reform had removed some cult objects (2 Kings 18:4), so Isaiah's hearers knew the issue was not imaginary.

a: Assyria will fall by a sword, not a man's
t: A sword not held by a man
p: Isaiah says Assyria will fall to no human army. The book tells the fulfillment in 37:36.
b: Judah's leaders expected Egypt's army to beat Assyria. Isaiah denies that any human sword will do it. Chapter 37 tells how "the angel of the LORD went out and struck the camp of Assyria" (37:36), and Sennacherib went home. The prophecies of 10:16–19, 10:33–34, 14:24–27, 17:12–14 and 30:31 point the same way. Assyria as an empire did not fall until 612 BC, to the Medes and Babylonians, which some readers see as the wider fulfillment. "Forced labor" (mas) means that Assyria's young men would end up as the conscript laborers that Assyria made of others.

a: His rock will pass away in terror
p: 'His rock' may be Assyria's king, its stronghold or its god. The Greek reads the line quite differently.
b: Sal'o, "his rock," is often taken as a title for the Assyrian king, the one his army leaned on, in mocking contrast with the LORD, Israel's Rock (17:10; 30:29). Others take it as Assyria's fortress, or its god. "Will pass away" can also mean "will run past" in panic. In the second line nes is the flag or battle standard, this site's word for it throughout Isaiah, and chattu means "be shattered, lose heart": the officers lose their nerve at the flag. The Greek has "they will be hemmed in by rock as by a stockade," a different reading of the same letters.

a: who has a fire in Zion
t: A fire and a furnace in Jerusalem
p: The LORD's fire in Zion is the altar fire of his house, and it burns his enemies.
b: 'Ur (fire) and tannur (oven, furnace) recall the altar hearth in the Temple court. Isaiah calls Jerusalem "Ariel" in 29:1–2, probably "altar hearth." The God who lives there is "a devouring fire" (Deuteronomy 4:24; 10:17; 30:27, 33). That fire protects Zion against Assyria here. In 33:14 the sinners in Zion itself ask who can live beside it.

a: A king will reign for the sake of righteousness
p: The just king of 32:1–8 has been read as Hezekiah, as an ideal ruler, and as the Messiah.
b: Hezekiah. Medieval Jewish commentators such as Rashi and Radak took the king as Hezekiah, the faithful king of chapters 36–39, with his officials ruling justly after the corrupt men of Ahaz's court. An ideal. Many modern scholars read 32:1–8 as a short wisdom poem about what good government looks like, close in style to Proverbs (note the words for fool and noble in 32:5–8). Some date it to Hezekiah's time, others to Josiah's reign (Hermann Barth) or later. The Messiah. Jerome and most church writers read it of Christ, whose kingdom brings justice and shelter, as in 9:6–7 and 11:1–5; Calvin saw Hezekiah's reign as a first, partial fulfillment pointing beyond itself. The verse itself says "a king," without a name.

a: Each of them will be like a hideout from the wind
p: Hebrew 'ish can mean 'each' (the king and his officials) or 'a man', and the KJV's 'a man' was read of Christ.
b: After "a king" and "officials" in 32:1, 'ish most likely means "each one" of them: good rulers are like shelter for the people. The KJV's "a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind" made the line a famous verse about one man, read by Christians as Christ the refuge. Both senses are possible. The images come from desert life: shade of a great rock in the heat, water channels in dry ground. Bad rulers had done the opposite (3:12–15; 10:1–2).

a: will not be pasted shut
p: Isaiah was sent to 'paste their eyes shut' (6:10). Here the same root returns, and the eyes open.
b: At his call Isaiah was told, "Make this people's heart fat, / make their ears heavy, / and paste their eyes shut" (6:10). The verb here comes from the same root, sha'a', to smear or paste over. Under the just king the hardening ends: eyes see, ears listen, rash minds understand, stammering tongues speak plainly (32:4). The book keeps coming back to this reversal (29:18; 35:5; 42:7, 18). The Masoretic pointing could also be read as "will not look away," but the link with 6:10 is widely recognized.

a: The godless fool will no longer be called noble
p: Wisdom words: nabal (the godless fool), kilay (the crook) and nadiv (the noble, generous person).
b: This little poem uses the vocabulary of Proverbs. Nabal is the fool who has no regard for God or decency, as in "the fool" of Psalm 14:1 and the outrage (nevalah) of 32:6; this site renders it "godless fool" as in Proverbs. Kilay, found only here and in 32:7, seems to mean a cheat or swindler (KJV "churl"). Nadiv means noble by birth and also generous in heart, and 32:8 plays on it three times. Under the coming king, words will match reality again. In 32:6 a different word, chonef, is rendered "act impiously," and chanefim in 33:14 "the impious," to keep the two Hebrew words apart.

a: The crook's tools are evil
p: 'The crook's tools', kelay kelav, is a sound play that English cannot keep.
b: Kelay ("crook") and kelav ("his tools, his weapons") sound almost alike, as if to say the man is his methods. His target is the poor and the needy, whose just claims he defeats "with false words" in court. This is the same complaint Isaiah made in 10:1–2 and 29:21. The written Hebrew (Ketiv) has 'anawim, "the humble," where the reading tradition (Qere) has 'aniyyim, "the poor"; both mean the powerless.

a: Women without a care, stand up and hear my voice!
p: As in 3:16–4:1, Isaiah turns to the wealthy women of Jerusalem and warns them of mourning to come.
b: The two words, sha'ananot ("at ease, carefree") and botechot ("so sure, trusting"), are not bad in themselves; the second is the verb "trust" (batach) that runs through chapters 30–37. These women trust the wrong thing, the harvest and the city walls. Amos had called the rich women of Samaria "cows of Bashan" (Amos 4:1). Isaiah calls on them to strip, put on sackcloth and lament, as women did at funerals (Jeremiah 9:17–20). The occasion is probably Sennacherib's invasion of 701, which wrecked a year's harvest (37:30).

a: In a year and a few days
p: Hebrew 'days upon a year' means a short time, a year and more. The KJV's 'many days and years' is a misreading.
b: The idiom yamim 'al-shanah (literally "days on a year") sets a near date: within about a year. The harvest that will fail is the grape and fruit harvest of autumn, the joyful time of the Feast of Booths. That fits an invading army that strips the land, as Sennacherib's did in 701 (compare 37:30, where the land needs two years to recover). The KJV's "Many days and years" takes the phrase as long duration, which most translators now reject.

a: The Ophel and the watchtower
p: The Ophel was the fortified hill between the City of David and the Temple, at the heart of royal Jerusalem.
b: 'Ofel means a swelling or mound, and in Jerusalem it named the high ground just south of the Temple, where the palace and government buildings stood. Jotham and Manasseh built walls on it (2 Chronicles 27:3; 33:14), and Nehemiah's builders repaired near it (Nehemiah 3:26–27). Bachan, "watchtower," is rare and is often explained as a loanword from Egyptian for a fortified tower. Isaiah pictures the seat of power turned into caves and grazing land for wild donkeys. Micah gave the same warning about Zion becoming a plowed field (Micah 3:12).

a: until a spirit from on high is poured out on us
p: Hebrew has 'spirit' with no 'the'. Christians read it of the Holy Spirit; the text speaks of God's life-giving breath.
b: Ruach can mean wind, breath or spirit. Here it comes "from on high" and is "poured out" like rain, and its effect is new life in a ruined land: wilderness becomes garden land. The same picture returns in 44:3 ("On your children I will pour out my Spirit"), Ezekiel 39:29 and Joel 2:28–29, which Peter quoted at Pentecost (Acts 2:17–18). This translation writes "a spirit," lower case, because here the Hebrew has no "my" or "the" and does not decide whether a person is meant; 44:3, where God says "my Spirit," is capitalized. Christian readers have seen here the gift of the Holy Spirit. Jewish readers have read it of the renewal of the messianic age. "Until" ties the gift to the end of the ruin described in 32:14.
orig: עַד־יֵעָרֶה עָלֵינוּ רוּחַ מִמָּרוֹם ('ad-ye'areh 'alenu ruach mimmarom)

a: garden land
p: Karmel means an orchard or fertile land, and is also the name of Mount Carmel.
b: The word karmel means a planted, fruitful place, "God's vineyard" as some explain it (kerem, vineyard, plus 'el). The ridge of Mount Carmel took its name from its green slopes, and Isaiah uses both senses: Carmel as a place withers in 33:9 and gets its glory back in 35:2. The line plays on a reversal found also in 29:17: wilderness becomes garden land, and garden land becomes like a forest.

a: What righteousness makes will be peace
t: Peace as the fruit of righteousness
p: Peace is not the absence of war here but what comes from right dealing.
b: Shalom means wholeness and well-being, and Isaiah says it grows out of tsedaqah, right relationships and fair dealing. The second line adds hashqet (quiet) and betach (safety, security), the very things Judah sought from Egypt (30:15 had offered them through quiet trust). James 3:18 echoes the thought: in the KJV, "the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace." Psalm 85:10 pictures righteousness and peace kissing.

a: But hail will fall as the forest falls
p: One of Isaiah's hardest verses: a sound play on hail, a falling forest and a city brought low.
b: The Hebrew plays on sound: barad (hail) and beredet (going down), kept here as "fall ... falls"; shiflah and tishpal (low, laid low). Which forest and which city? Some read the forest as Assyria's army, felled like trees in 10:18–19 and 10:33–34, and the city as an enemy capital, as in 25:2 and 26:5. Others take it as Jerusalem, so the verse looks back to the ruin of 32:14 before the blessing of 32:20. Still others move it after 32:14. The Greek says hail "will not come upon you." No reading is certain.

a: Happy are you
p: Ashrei, 'happy', is the first word of the Psalms. Here it blesses farmers in a land at peace.
b: Ashrekhem, "happy are you," is the word that opens the Psalter (Psalm 1:1); older versions render it "blessed." The picture is a land with water everywhere and no enemy: farmers sow beside every water and let their ox and donkey roam without fear of raiders or of trampled crops. After the lament of 32:9–14, the section ends with peace on the farm, the kind Isaiah's hearers would have felt in their bones.

a: Woe to you, plunderer
p: The last of Isaiah's six woes (28–33) is aimed at an unnamed plunderer, most likely Assyria.
b: The six woes of chapters 28–33 begin at 28:1 and 29:1, 15, 30:1 and 31:1, and end here. The first five target Israel and Judah; this one turns against the enemy. Most readers take the plunderer to be Assyria, which had taken Hezekiah's tribute and then attacked anyway (see 33:8). Some scholars think chapter 33 was shaped later, so that the plunderer stands for any empire that crushes God's people, Babylon or later Persia. The words fit any of them, which may be the point: a destroyer will be destroyed.

a: you double-crosser, whom no one double-crossed
p: Shoded and boged, plunderer and double-crosser, are paired here as in 21:2; 24:16 piles up bagad.
b: Shadad means to devastate or plunder, and bagad to deal treacherously, to break faith. Isaiah uses the same pair in 21:2 ("the double-crosser double-crosses, / the plunderer plunders"), and 24:16 piles up bagad five times; this site renders the words the same way in all three places. The repetition in this verse is the poetic justice of the law of retaliation: what the destroyer does will be done to him. The Greek turns the verse into a curse on those who trouble "you" (Jerusalem), and ends with an image of moths in a garment.

a: LORD, show us grace
p: Chapter 33 mixes prophecy with the people's prayer, like a psalm used in worship.
b: The voice changes from the prophet to "us": the community prays, as in the psalms of lament (Psalm 123:3: "Be gracious to us, LORD, be gracious to us!"). In 1924 Hermann Gunkel called chapter 33 a "prophetic liturgy": prayer (33:2–4), confession of trust (33:5–6), lament (33:7–9), God's answer (33:10–13), a gate liturgy asking who may live with God (33:14–16), and a vision of the future (33:17–24). "Morning by morning" recalls the morning as the time of God's help (Psalm 46:5; Lamentations 3:23).

a: the fear of the LORD, that is his treasure
p: The fear of the LORD, the starting point of wisdom, is the real wealth of the city or of its king.
b: Proverbs opens with "The fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins" (Proverbs 1:7), and Isaiah lists it among the gifts of the Spirit on the shoot of Jesse (11:2). Here it is the treasure, 'otsar, the word used for Hezekiah's storehouses in 39:2–4. The book seems to set the two side by side: Hezekiah's treasure house goes to Babylon, but the fear of the LORD is the treasure no envoy can carry off. "His" is unclear: it may be the people's ("your times"), Zion's, or the king's.

a: Their heroes shout from outside
p: 'Er'ellam appears only here. It is usually taken as 'their heroes', but no one is sure.
b: The word may come from 'ari'el, "lion of God," used for a hero in 2 Samuel 23:20, or it may be linked with Ariel, Isaiah's name for Jerusalem (29:1). Some read "the men of Ariel." The Great Isaiah Scroll writes the letters as two words, which can be read "I will appear to them." The Greek has "in your fear these will be afraid." The parallel line makes the general sense plain: the strong and the diplomats weep, because the peace they worked for has failed.

a: the messengers who went for peace weep
p: Many readers see here the tribute Hezekiah paid in 701 and Sennacherib's attack that followed.
b: 2 Kings 18:14–16 tells that Hezekiah sent word to Sennacherib at Lachish, "I have done wrong," and paid a huge tribute, stripping the temple doors. Yet the Rabshakeh still came to Jerusalem's wall (2 Kings 18:17). If that is the setting, "A treaty has been broken" (33:8) is the Assyrian king breaking his word after taking the money. Isaiah's book, which leaves out the tribute in chapter 36, may remember it here. The lines also fit any time when diplomacy failed, and the chapter does not name names.

a: Sharon has become like the desert plain
t: The land mourns, and will bloom
p: Lebanon, Sharon, Bashan and Carmel wither here; in 35:2 the same names come back in glory.
b: These were the greenest places Isaiah's hearers knew: the cedar forests of Lebanon, the coastal plain of Sharon, the oak woods and pastures of Bashan east of the Jordan, and the slopes of Carmel. "The land dries up" ('aval) can also mean "the land mourns": the earth itself grieves. The 'aravah, "desert plain," is the dry rift valley south of the Dead Sea. Chapter 35 answers this verse point for point: "Lebanon's glory is given to it, / and the beauty of Carmel and of Sharon" (35:2).

a: Now I will rise up, says the LORD
p: God's 'now' answers the lament, as in Psalm 12:5.
b: The triple 'attah, "now," marks the turning point of the chapter. The words echo Psalm 12:5, where the LORD says, "so now I will get up." The verbs "rise, stand tall, lift myself high" are the language of 6:1, where the Lord sat on a throne "high and lifted up," and of 2:11–17, where on the day of the LORD he alone is lifted high. When the LORD rises, nations scatter (33:3).

a: You conceive dry grass
p: The enemy's plans are a pregnancy that produces only straw, and their own breath sets it on fire.
b: Dry grass and stubble burn in a moment. The picture is of schemes that come to nothing and then destroy their makers: "your breath is a fire." Isaiah used the image of a failed birth for his own people in 26:18, where they give birth only to wind, and 59:4 and Psalm 7:14 speak of conceiving trouble and giving birth to lies. The next verse turns the fire into lime kilns.

a: Peoples will become lime in the kiln
p: Limestone was burned in kilns to make lime for plaster; the fire had to be fierce and long.
b: Burning limestone, and sometimes bones, at high heat produced quicklime for plaster and whitewash (Deuteronomy 27:2, 4). Amos condemned Moab for burning an Edomite king's bones to lime (Amos 2:1). The comparison means total destruction, nothing left but white powder. Thornbushes, used as quick fuel, add the picture of a fire that flares up and is gone.

a: Which of us can stay beside a fire that devours?
p: A gate liturgy like Psalms 15 and 24: the question who may come into God's presence, and the answer in 33:15.
b: The verb gur means to live as a guest or resident alien, and it is the verb of Psalm 15:1: "LORD, who is welcome as a guest in your tent?" Psalm 24:3 asks "Who can climb the LORD's mountain?" In both, the answer is a list of moral qualities, and 33:15 gives such a list. The new thing here is that the God of Zion is a fire (31:9; Deuteronomy 4:24: "the LORD your God is a devouring fire"). Sinners in Zion realize that his presence, which protects the city from Assyria, is a danger to them too. Hebrews 12:29 repeats Deuteronomy's picture of God as fire.

a: flames that burn forever
p: The KJV's 'everlasting burnings' is often read as hell. In context it is God's holy presence in Zion.
b: Preachers have often quoted the KJV's "Who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?" as a question about hell. But the people asking are the sinners "in Zion," and the fire is the one the LORD keeps "in Zion" and "in Jerusalem" (31:9). The question is whether anyone can live near the holy God, as in 6:5 ("Woe to me! I am finished"). The answer in 33:15–16 is not an escape from the fire but a life lived rightly, which lets a person "live on the heights" in its presence. Later Christian and Jewish writers did use Isaiah's fire imagery for final judgment (66:24).

a: The one who walks in what is right
p: The Talmud says that David summed up the law's 613 commands in eleven (Psalm 15), and Isaiah in six (33:15).
b: A well-known passage of the Babylonian Talmud (Makkot 24a) says the 613 commands given to Moses were brought down to eleven by David in Psalm 15, to six by Isaiah in this verse, to three by Micah (Micah 6:8), to two by Isaiah again (56:1), and to one by Amos, who gives the single command to seek God and live (Amos 5:4). Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak offers Habakkuk instead, with its line that the righteous live by faithfulness (Habakkuk 2:4). The six are: walking in righteousness, speaking what is straight, refusing extortion, refusing bribes, closing the ears to talk of bloodshed, and closing the eyes to evil. "Talk of blood" means plots to kill or to ruin someone by false testimony (Proverbs 1:11).

a: A king in his beauty
p: The king in his beauty may be the LORD himself (33:22), the just king of 32:1, or the Messiah.
b: The next verses look back on the terror of the siege, when the people saw Assyria's officials and Hezekiah in sackcloth (37:1). Now they will see a king "in his beauty." Many commentators take the king to be the LORD, since 33:22 says "the LORD is our king," and since Isaiah saw "the King, the LORD of Armies" in 6:5. Others think of a human king of David's line, as in 32:1, perhaps Hezekiah restored after the crisis. Christian readers have seen Christ, the king in whom God's beauty is seen, and a familiar hymn line draws on the KJV's "Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty." "A land of far horizons" means borders pushed far out, no longer a besieged city.

a: Where is the clerk?
p: The Assyrian officials who counted tribute and towers are gone. Paul echoes this question in 1 Corinthians 1:20.
b: The sofer (clerk, scribe) and the shoqel (one who weighs) are the officials who recorded and weighed tribute; Assyrian reliefs often show scribes with tablet and scroll counting booty. "The one who took count of the towers" was sizing up the walls for a siege. Their questions now echo in an empty place. The Greek reads "Where are the scribes? Where are the counselors?" Paul combines this line with 19:12 when he asks, in the KJV, "Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world?" (1 Corinthians 1:20), turning Isaiah's taunt against human wisdom that rejects the cross.

a: whose tongue stammers with no sense in it
p: The Assyrians' foreign speech, the 'stammering lips' of 28:11, will be heard no more.
b: Assyrian (a dialect of Akkadian) was a Semitic language, a distant cousin of Hebrew, but far enough from it that ordinary people could not follow it. In 28:11 Isaiah warned that God would speak to his people through stammering lips and a foreign tongue, the speech of invaders, a line Paul applies to speaking in tongues (1 Corinthians 14:21). Here the threat is lifted. Deuteronomy 28:49 had warned of a nation from far off whose language Israel would not understand.

a: a tent no one will pack up
p: Jerusalem is pictured as a tent whose pegs will never be pulled up, unlike the nomad's tent of 38:12.
b: In Israel's memory God's dwelling was a tent that moved from place to place in the wilderness (2 Samuel 7:6). Zion is a tent that stays: its pegs are never pulled and its ropes never snap. The picture draws on the Zion psalms (Psalm 46; Psalm 48) and the promise to David. The same book later uses a tent to picture life itself pulled up and taken away, in Hezekiah's psalm (38:12), and 54:2 calls Zion to stretch its tent wider. "Our festival city" recalls the pilgrim feasts that brought Judah to Jerusalem.

a: a place of rivers, of streams wide on both sides
t: Rivers in a city with none
p: Jerusalem had no river. Isaiah pictures the LORD himself as its broad river, a moat no warship can cross.
b: Great cities like Nineveh, Babylon and Thebes stood on rivers that brought trade and defense (Nahum 3:8). Jerusalem had only the Gihon spring and Hezekiah's tunnel. Isaiah says the LORD will be to his city what rivers were to others, but better: no enemy galley can sail on them. The Zion psalms had already sung of "A river! Its channels gladden the city of God" (Psalm 46:4), and Ezekiel 47 and Revelation 22:1 picture a river flowing from God's throne. The word 'addir, "majestic," is used for the LORD and then for the ship that cannot pass: majesty belongs to him alone.

a: the LORD is our commander
p: Mechoqeq can mean a lawgiver or a ruler with a staff of command. The KJV has 'lawgiver'.
b: Mechoqeq comes from chaqaq, to inscribe or decree, and can mean "lawgiver" (so the KJV). But in Genesis 49:10 and Judges 5:14 it means a ruler's staff or a commander, and Deuteronomy 33:21 uses it of a leader's portion. Between "judge" and "king," a title of leadership fits best, and this translation renders it "commander." Either way, the three titles together say that the LORD fills every office that rules and rescues his people, which is why the verse ends, "He is the one who will save us."

a: For the LORD is our judge
p: A popular claim says this verse gave the United States its three branches of government. There is no evidence for it.
b: Using the KJV's "the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king," a claim repeated in popular books, sermons and websites on America's Christian heritage says that the founders took the judicial, legislative and executive branches from this verse. There is no evidence for it in the records of the Constitutional Convention, in The Federalist or in the ratification debates. Madison's defense of separated powers in The Federalist No. 47 names Montesquieu as "the oracle who is always consulted and cited on this subject." Isaiah's verse does not separate powers at all: it gives all three to the LORD.

a: Your ropes have gone slack
p: The image jumps to a ship with slack rigging, probably the enemy pictured as the galley of 33:21.
b: Who is "you"? Most take the enemy (Assyria), just compared to a warship that cannot cross Zion's waters (33:21): its ropes hang loose, the mast wobbles, no sail can be spread. So its cargo becomes plunder, and even the lame of Jerusalem can carry some off. Others take "you" as Zion, weak as a crippled ship but still given the spoil. Some move the first half of the verse to follow 33:21. The point is the reversal: the weakest in Jerusalem share the spoil of the strongest empire (compare 2 Kings 7:16).

a: none who live there will say, "I am sick"
p: The chapter ends by tying health to forgiveness, a link the book then plays out in Hezekiah's illness.
b: Psalm 103:3 sets the two side by side: "He pardons every wrong you have done; / he heals every sickness you have." Isaiah's last line pictures a city where no one is sick, because guilt is "lifted away" (nasa', "lift, carry"), the word for bearing guilt in 53:12. In the book's order, the next time Jerusalem's king is sick (38:1), he is healed and confesses that God has "flung" all his sins behind his back (38:17). The Gospels join the two in the healing of the paralyzed man (Mark 2:5–12).

a: Nations, come close and hear!
t: A summons to the whole world
p: Chapter 34 opens like a court case in which the world is called to hear its sentence.
b: Isaiah opened his book by calling heaven and earth as witnesses against Judah (1:2). Here every nation and "the world, with all it brings forth" are summoned to hear judgment on themselves. The verse names all the nations (34:2) before it narrows to Edom (34:5). Psalm 49:1 and Micah 1:2 use the same kind of summons. Chapters 34 and 35 form a pair: judgment on the world, typified by Edom, and then the desert in bloom for the ransomed.

a: He has put them under the ban
p: Cherem, 'the ban', meant devoting a city to God by its total destruction. Here God does it to the nations.
b: Hecherim is the verb of cherem, the practice of holy war in which a city and its goods were "devoted" to God and destroyed (Deuteronomy 7:2; Joshua 6:21). This site renders it "put under the ban." In 2 Kings 19:11 (= 37:11) the Assyrians claimed it as their own right. Here the LORD is the one who places whole armies under it, and 34:5 calls Edom "the people under my ban." The language of slaughter and sacrifice in 34:5–7 belongs to the same picture.

a: the sky will roll up like a scroll
p: Revelation 6:14 uses this picture for the end, and Jesus's words on the last days draw on the verse.
b: An ancient book was a scroll; rolling it up meant the reading was over. Isaiah pictures the sky rolled up and the stars falling like dead leaves and shriveled figs. Revelation joins the two images: "The stars in the sky fell to the earth, like unripe figs falling from a fig tree" and "The sky split apart like a scroll being rolled up" (Revelation 6:13–14). The Greek of Isaiah has "all the powers of the heavens will melt," and Jesus's warning that "the powers in the heavens will be shaken" (Matthew 24:29) echoes it, with 13:10. See also Psalm 102:26 and 2 Peter 3:10–12. Whether the language is literal or a picture of political collapse is debated (see the chapter page).
r: Revelation 6:13–14; Matthew 24:29; Mark 13:24–25; 13:10; Psalm 102:26; 2 Peter 3:10–12; Hebrews 1:11–12

a: The whole army of heaven will rot
p: Tseva' hashamayim, 'the army of heaven', means the stars, which many of Judah's neighbors worshiped.
b: The phrase means the sun, moon and stars, seen as ranks of soldiers, and sometimes the heavenly beings behind them (1 Kings 22:19). Israel was forbidden to worship them (Deuteronomy 4:19), but Manasseh, Hezekiah's son, built altars to them (2 Kings 21:3–5), and Josiah tore them down (2 Kings 23:4–5). "Rot" (namaq) is a strange word to use of stars: it means to decay or melt away. The powers the nations trusted dissolve with them. This site renders tseva' "army," matching "the LORD of Armies."

a: it will come down on Edom
p: Edom stands out for its part in Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC, and it became a symbol of every enemy.
b: Edom, Judah's neighbor southeast of the Dead Sea, was descended from Esau, Jacob's brother (Genesis 36). When Babylon took Jerusalem in 586 BC, Edomites cheered and joined in (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 10–14; Lamentations 4:21–22; Ezekiel 35). For this reason most critical scholars date chapter 34 after 586, and see Edom here as the pattern of all God's enemies. Traditional scholars note that Edom had long been hostile (2 Kings 8:20–22; 2 Chronicles 28:17, in Ahaz's day) and that Isaiah names it in 21:11–12. In later Jewish interpretation "Edom" came to stand for Rome, and medieval commentators such as Radak read the chapter of Rome and of Christian Europe. Chapter 63 returns to the scene: "Who is this coming in from Edom, / from Bozrah in clothes dyed red?" (63:1).
r: Genesis 36:1; Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 10–14; Lamentations 4:21–22; Ezekiel 35; 21:11–12; 63:1–6; Malachi 1:2–4

a: In Bozrah the LORD holds a sacrifice
p: Bozrah, Edom's capital, is the modern village of Buseirah in southern Jordan, excavated in the 1970s.
b: Bozrah stood on a spur near the King's Highway, in the hills southeast of the Dead Sea. Excavations led by Crystal-M. Bennett from 1971 to 1980 found a fortified town with large public buildings, flourishing mainly in the 600s and 500s BC, when Edom was a vassal of Assyria and then of Babylon. The name sounds like batsir, "grape harvest," which may lie behind the winepress picture of 63:1–3. The verse turns war into a sacrifice: lambs, goats and rams' fat are the people of Edom, and the LORD's sword is the priest's knife (compare Jeremiah 46:10; Zephaniah 1:7).

a: Wild oxen
p: Re'em is the aurochs, a huge wild ox. The KJV's 'unicorns' comes from the Greek monokeros.
b: The re'em was the aurochs, the wild ancestor of cattle, which Assyrian kings hunted and pictured in their palaces; Akkadian rimu is the same word. The Greek translators of other books rendered it monokeros, "one-horned," perhaps because animals in side view show one horn, and the Latin unicornis and the KJV's "unicorns" followed. The Greek of this verse has "the mighty ones" instead. Here the wild oxen and bulls stand, like the lambs and rams of 34:6, for the strong men of Edom.

a: the LORD's day of vengeance
p: The same pairing of 'day of vengeance' and 'year' returns in 61:2 and 63:4, and Jesus stops before it in Luke 4.
b: Naqam is not personal spite but the vindication a judge or king gives to the wronged: here "to win Zion's case" (riv, a lawsuit). The pairing "day ... year" returns twice in Isaiah: "a year of the LORD's goodwill / and a day of our God's vengeance" (61:2), and "For a day of vengeance was on my mind, / and the year to redeem my own had come" (63:4). In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus read 61:1–2 but stopped before "the day of vengeance" (Luke 4:18–19). Chapter 35:4 gives the other side of the same day: vengeance on the enemy is rescue for God's people.

a: Its wadis will change to tar
p: Pitch and sulfur recall Sodom and Gomorrah, near Edom's border at the Dead Sea.
b: "Then the LORD rained sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, from the LORD, out of the sky" (Genesis 19:24). The Dead Sea region was known for bitumen (tar) pits (Genesis 14:10), so the picture comes from Edom's own neighborhood. Deuteronomy 29:23 warns that Israel's land could become "sulfur and salt" like Sodom, and Jeremiah 49:18 says the same of Edom. Isaiah had compared Jerusalem to Sodom in 1:9–10. Revelation 14:10–11 and 19:20 draw on the burning sulfur.
r: Genesis 19:24; Genesis 14:10; Deuteronomy 29:23; Jeremiah 49:17–18; 1:9–10; Revelation 14:10–11; Revelation 19:20

a: its smoke will keep going up forever
p: Revelation uses this line for Babylon and for those who worship the beast. What does 'forever' mean here?
b: Revelation borrows the words twice: "The smoke of their torment rises forever and ever" (Revelation 14:11) and "The smoke from her goes up forever and ever" (Revelation 19:3). Many Christian readers take them as a picture of everlasting punishment. Others, including those who hold that the wicked are finally destroyed (conditional immortality), point out that in Isaiah the burning land then becomes a home for owls, jackals and hyenas (34:11–15). For them "forever" here means a ruin that is never rebuilt, as with Sodom, whose smoke has long since stopped (Jude 7). Both sides agree that Isaiah's image is of complete and lasting judgment.

a: a measuring line of shapelessness
p: Tohu and bohu, 'shapeless and empty', are the words of Genesis 1:2. Edom returns to the state before creation.
b: "The earth was shapeless and empty" (Genesis 1:2): the Hebrew pair tohu wabohu appears only there, in Jeremiah 4:23 ("I looked at the earth, and it was shapeless and empty") and here, split across two lines. A builder's measuring line and plumb stones were used to lay out a house (28:17; 2 Kings 21:13). God uses them here to lay out unmaking: the land is measured not for building but for chaos. Creation's order is reversed, and the land goes back to wild creatures.

a: Desert owl and hedgehog
p: The names of the birds and beasts in 34:11–15 are uncertain, and translations differ widely.
b: Hebrew animal names are often guesses. Qa'at has been read as pelican, cormorant (KJV) or desert owl; qippod as hedgehog, porcupine or bittern (KJV); yanshuf as owl or ibis (this translation follows the Greek, ibis, to keep it apart from the owl of 34:15 and the KJV's "screech owl" for Lilith); qippoz (34:15) as owl or arrow snake. Zephaniah 2:14 uses the same pair for ruined Nineveh. Most were unclean animals (Leviticus 11:13–19), and all are creatures of empty places. Revelation draws on the scene: Babylon "has become a home for demons ... a prison for every unclean bird" (Revelation 18:2).

a: a goat-demon will call out to its fellow
p: Sa'ir means a male goat, but it also names goat-shaped beings of the desert. The Greek has 'demons' in this verse.
b: Sa'ir, "hairy one," is the ordinary word for a male goat (Leviticus 4:23), and many translations read "wild goat" here, one more animal of the ruins. But the word also names goat-shaped beings of the desert: in Leviticus 17:7 Israel must stop sacrificing "to the goat idols," as this site renders it there, and 2 Chronicles 11:15 has Jeroboam appoint priests for them. In 13:21, in ruined Babylon, this site has "goat-demons" (KJV "satyrs"), and the singular here follows it, since Lilith appears in the next line. The Greek renders the verse with daimonia (demons) and onokentauroi, donkey-centaurs. Whether Isaiah meant animals, spirits or both, the point is a land given over to everything that lives outside human order.

a: Lilith
p: Lilit, found only here in the Bible, is the name of a female night demon of Mesopotamian and later Jewish belief.
b: The word. Akkadian texts name wind or night demons, lilu and lilitu, who prey on men and newborns. Hebrew lilit is almost certainly the same figure, though Hebrew ears heard layil, "night," in it. The translations. The Greek has "donkey-centaurs"; Jerome's Latin has lamia, a child-snatching monster of Greek legend; the KJV has "screech owl"; several modern versions describe a nocturnal animal instead of giving a name; the JPS Tanakh and the NRSV keep "Lilith." The Great Isaiah Scroll has a plural, liliyyot. Later lore. At Qumran, the Songs of the Sage (4Q510) list "liliths" among demons to be driven off; the Talmud warns that a man sleeping alone may be seized by Lilith (Bavli Shabbat 151b); the medieval Alphabet of Ben Sira made her Adam's first wife. Verdict. Isaiah borrows a figure his hearers knew to say that ruined Edom will belong to the creatures of the night. The later legends are not in the verse.

a: Look it up in the LORD's scroll, and read
p: The 'LORD's scroll' may be this prophecy itself, a heavenly record, or the Scriptures read so far.
b: This prophecy. Many take it as Isaiah's own written oracle: readers in later days are invited to check it against what happened to Edom. Isaiah was told to write his words for a coming day (8:16; 30:8). A heavenly book. Others think of God's book in which creatures and events are recorded (Psalm 139:16; Malachi 3:16). Scripture. Some see one of the earliest references to a written collection of the LORD's words being searched and read, a habit of later Jewish study. The point is that God's word is exact: not one of the creatures assigned to Edom will be missing. The command comes "from my mouth": the prophet speaks for God (see the variant).

a: his hand measured out their shares with the line
p: The language of Joshua's land division is used to give Edom to wild animals.
b: In Joshua, the land was divided by lot and measured out to the tribes for all generations (Joshua 18:6, 10; Numbers 26:55). Here God does the same for jackals, owls and kites. Edom becomes their permanent inheritance, the reverse of a nation receiving its land. "Generation after generation" matches 34:10: as no human will pass through, the animals will hold it. Malachi 1:3 says, in another way, that Edom's hill country was given over to desert jackals.

a: they will live in it from one generation to the next
t: A seam in the Great Isaiah Scroll
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll splits Isaiah in two after chapter 33, and the words around 34:17–35:2 are in another hand.
b: In the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) column 27 ends with chapter 33 and three blank lines, and chapter 34 begins at the top of column 28. Many scholars (Tov among them) think a second scribe took over there; others think one scribe copied the scroll in two stages. Within column 28, the text from the end of 34:17 into 35:2 is written by a different hand, in a space the first copyist left. Eugene Ulrich and Peter Flint list it among places where the scroll first lacked words that are in the Masoretic Text. Drew Longacre explains these gaps by a damaged master copy. The scroll's wording here does not differ in meaning. Some have connected the split after chapter 33 to the old idea that Isaiah was copied in two halves.

a: like the crocus
p: Chavatselet is a spring flower of the bulb family, probably a crocus or asphodel. The KJV has 'rose'.
b: The KJV's "the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose" became famous, and the same word is "the rose of Sharon" in the KJV of Song of Songs 2:1. Roses as we know them did not grow wild in the Judean desert. Chavatselet is probably related to batsal, "bulb," and means a flower that springs up from a bulb after rain, like the crocus or the asphodel. Hebrew yesusum at the start of the verse has an odd final letter; the KJV took it as "shall be glad for them," but most read it simply as "will be glad."

a: Lebanon's glory is given to it
p: The names that withered in 33:9 return: Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon give their glory to the desert.
b: In 33:9, "Lebanon, ashamed, shrivels; / Sharon has become like the desert plain, / and Bashan and Carmel shake themselves bare." Now the desert itself receives their glory. The pictures of 32:15 return as well: wilderness turned garden land. The theme runs through the second half of Isaiah: "I will turn the wilderness into a pond" (41:18), and "He makes her wilderness like Eden" (51:3).

a: These are the ones who will see the LORD's glory
p: In 40:5 all flesh will see the LORD's glory; here it is revealed first in the blooming desert.
b: The seraphs sang that the whole earth is full of the LORD's glory (6:3), but Judah could not see it. In 40:5, "Then the LORD's glory will be revealed, / and all flesh will see it, all together." Here those who see are the desert places themselves, or the people who walk through them (35:4). "The beauty of our God" (hadar) is the word for a king's splendor. Chapter 35 reads like a preview of 40:1–11, and many scholars think it was written to join the two halves of the book (see 35:10).

a: Put strength into slack hands
p: Hebrews 12:12 quotes this line to encourage Christians who are worn down by suffering.
b: Limp hands and wobbly knees picture people too discouraged to act or stand (Job 4:3–4; Ezekiel 7:17). The command is plural: the hearers are to strengthen one another. The letter to the Hebrews picks it up, telling its readers to brace their weak hands and knees and to make level paths for their feet (Hebrews 12:12–13, which also draws on Proverbs 4:26). There it follows the call to run the race with endurance, looking to Jesus.

a: Look, your God! Vengeance is coming
p: The same cry is the good news of 40:9, and vengeance on the enemy means rescue for the fearful.
b: "Tell the towns of Judah, / 'Look, your God!'" (40:9): the same two Hebrew words, hinneh 'elohekhem, are the heart of both passages. "Those whose hearts are pounding" (literally "hasty of heart") are people in panic, like Ahaz and his court in 7:2–4, whom Isaiah told, "Don't be afraid." The "vengeance" and "repayment" are the same as in 34:8, seen from the other side: for Edom judgment, for God's people rescue. "He is coming himself": God does not send help; he comes.

a: Then blind people's eyes will open
p: Jesus answered John the Baptist's question with this verse and 61:1: the blind see, the lame walk, the deaf hear.
b: When John asked from prison whether Jesus was the one to come, Jesus answered: "The blind see again and the lame walk. People with skin disease are made clean and the deaf hear. The dead are raised, and the poor are told the good news" (Matthew 11:5; Luke 7:22). The list blends 35:5–6 with 26:19, 29:18 and 61:1. Matthew 15:31 describes the crowd seeing "speechless people talking, twisted limbs made sound, lame people walking about and blind people seeing." A Qumran text, the Messianic Apocalypse (4Q521), shows that some Jews already expected such healings in the days of God's anointed. In Isaiah the healings also reverse the blindness and deafness God sent on his people (6:9–10; 32:3).

a: a mute tongue will sing out
p: The Greek here uses mogilalos, 'speaking with difficulty', found in the New Testament only in Mark 7:32.
b: In Mark 7:32 people bring Jesus a deaf man "who spoke with difficulty," mogilalos, and when he is healed the crowd marvels that he makes the deaf hear and the speechless talk (Mark 7:37). The rare Greek word appears in the Greek Old Testament only here, in Isaiah 35:6, so many scholars think Mark meant his readers to hear Isaiah's promise. Likewise the lame man in Acts 3:8 goes, in the KJV's words, "walking, and leaping, and praising God," like the lame man who "will jump like a deer."

a: The shimmering heat
p: Sharav is the shimmer of heat over the desert, the mirage that looks like water.
b: Sharav is related to Arabic sarab, "mirage." Travelers in the desert see what looks like a lake and find only burning sand. Isaiah promises that the false water will become real water. The word appears again only in 49:10, where the returning exiles are spared the scorching heat. "Where jackals used to lie" is the reverse of 34:13, where Edom becomes "a den for jackals."

a: the Holy Road
p: A raised road through the desert for the redeemed: the road of 11:16 and 40:3, and a picture of the new exodus.
b: Maslul, a built-up road, appears only here; the related mesillah is the "highway" of 11:16, 19:23, 40:3 ("make straight / a highway for our God") and 62:10. In the ancient world great processional ways led to temples, and pilgrims to Zion sang of "highways" in their hearts (Psalm 84:5). The road is holy, so nothing unclean may use it, like the camp of Israel in the wilderness. Early Christians called their faith "the Way" (Acts 9:2), and the Qumran community read 40:3 of its own life in the desert.

a: Those who walk the road will not go astray, even fools
t: A road even fools can follow
p: The last lines of 35:8 are unclear: the road is either too plain for anyone to lose, or closed to fools.
b: Word for word the Hebrew reads: "and it, for them; one walking a road, and fools will not wander." One reading, followed here, says the road is for God's people, and is so plain that even simple travelers will not lose their way. Another says fools ('evilim, the stubborn fools of Proverbs) will not wander onto it at all. The phrase "it will be theirs" (wehu lamo, "and it, for them") may refer to the redeemed of 35:9, or the text may be damaged. The Greek reads: "the dispersed will walk on it."
orig: וְהוּא־לָמוֹ הֹלֵךְ דֶּרֶךְ וֶאֱוִילִים לֹא יִתְעוּ (wehu-lamo holekh derekh we'evilim lo yit'u)

a: The redeemed will walk on it
p: Ge'ulim, 'the redeemed', and peduyim, 'the ransomed' (35:10), are key words of Isaiah 40–66.
b: Ga'al is the action of the go'el, the family redeemer who buys back a relative or his land (Leviticus 25:25; Ruth 4). When God is the go'el, this site writes "redeemer" (41:14; 43:14; 44:6). Padah (35:10) is the word for ransoming the firstborn and for God bringing Israel out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8). Both words in one place, together with the road through the wilderness, picture a second exodus. No lion will threaten them, unlike the road in 30:6.

a: The ransomed of the LORD will return
p: 35:10 returns word for word at 51:11, one of the reasons many scholars link chapter 35 with chapters 40–55.
b: The same lines stand at 35:10 and 51:11, and the Hebrew is nearly identical, so this site gives them the same English. Chapter 35's themes, the desert road, the blind and the deaf healed, "Look, your God!", and the return to Zion, are the themes of 40–55. Critical view. Most scholars think chapter 35 was written by or after the prophet of 40–55. Odil Hannes Steck argued that it was composed as a bridge joining the two halves of the book. Traditional view. Readers who hold one Isaiah see the prophet himself sounding the theme he will develop later. Either way, the verse ends the first half of the book's poetry with joy, and only the Hezekiah chapters stand between it and 40:1.

a: In King Hezekiah's fourteenth year
p: Isaiah 36–39 and 2 Kings 18:13–20:19 tell the same events in nearly the same words. Which came first?
b: Kings first. Most scholars since the 1800s have held that the chapters were written for Kings and copied into Isaiah, slightly shortened, to close the first half of the book. Isaiah first. Others, notably Christopher Seitz, argue that the story was shaped in Isaiah's circle and then taken into Kings. A common source. A third view has both books drawing on one prophetic narrative. 2 Chronicles 32:32 says Hezekiah's story was written "in the vision of the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz." The biggest difference is that Isaiah lacks 2 Kings 18:14–16, Hezekiah's surrender and tribute, so in Isaiah he is a king of trust with no lapse. Notes on 2 Kings 18–20 cover the shared history; the notes here deal with what Isaiah does differently.

a: Sennacherib king of Assyria marched on all the walled towns of Judah
p: Sennacherib's own records of the campaign of 701 BC survive on clay prisms; see the note on 2 Kings 18:13.
b: The Taylor Prism in the British Museum and the Oriental Institute Prism in Chicago (both from about 690 BC) give the Assyrian account: 46 walled towns of Hezekiah taken, 200,150 people carried off, and Hezekiah shut up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage," later paying tribute that was sent after the king to Nineveh. The annals never claim that Jerusalem fell. The chapter page sets the annals beside Isaiah's account, and the notes on 2 Kings 18:13–14 give the details.

a: He took his stand by the water channel of the Upper Pool
p: Isaiah's book sets Hezekiah's crisis at the very spot where Ahaz was offered a sign and refused (7:3).
b: In 7:3 the LORD told Isaiah to meet Ahaz "at the end of the water channel of the Upper Pool, on the main road to the Launderers' Field." There Ahaz, threatened by Aram and Israel, chose Assyria over trust in the LORD (7:9–12; 2 Kings 16:7). Now Assyria's officer stands on the same ground. Within Isaiah the two scenes form a pair: Ahaz the king who would not trust, Hezekiah the king who does. See the note on 2 Kings 18:17 for the place. Isaiah names only the Rabshakeh, not the other two officers of 2 Kings 18:17, and lacks Kings' twice-told "they went up and came to Jerusalem"; so its verb is singular, "he took his stand."

a: Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the palace
p: Isaiah 22:15–25 foretold that Eliakim would replace Shebna over the palace. Here the change has happened.
b: In 22:15 Isaiah was sent "to this steward, to Shebna, who is over the palace," to tell him he would be thrown out, and in 22:20 God says, "I will send for my servant Eliakim son of Hilkiah." In chapter 36 Eliakim holds the office and Shebna is the secretary, a lower post. Readers of the book can see the earlier word fulfilled. The note on 2 Kings 18:18 covers the offices and the seal impressions bearing such titles.

a: What is this trust of yours that you trust in?
p: The Rabshakeh's key word, batach 'trust', is also one of the key words of Isaiah's own message.
b: The speech uses the verb seven times in Kings and nearly as often here (see the note on 2 Kings 18:19). In Isaiah the word has a history. Judah was told, "in calm and in trust your strength will lie" (30:15), and "Woe to those going down to Egypt for help" who "trust in chariots" (31:1). The song of 12:2 has already given the answer: "I will trust and not be afraid." The Assyrian's question is the book's question: where does Judah put its trust?

a: a plan and strength for war
p: 'Counsel and strength' is a gift of the LORD's Spirit to the coming king in 11:2. Here it is the Assyrian's taunt.
b: The Hebrew 'etsah ugevurah are the same two words as in 11:2: "a spirit of counsel and strength." The Rabshakeh mocks Hezekiah's war plans as "mere words from your lips." Isaiah himself had attacked the court's plans that did not come from the LORD (29:15; 30:1). Within the book, true counsel and strength come from the LORD's Spirit, not from alliances. On "I say" here, where Kings has "you say," see the variant.

a: this crushed reed
p: The Rabshakeh calls Egypt a crushed reed. In 42:3 the LORD's servant will not snap a crushed reed.
b: The image is the same in Kings (see the note on 2 Kings 18:21). Isaiah's book reuses the words in a very different way: "A reed that is crushed he will not snap" (42:3). The Hebrew is the same phrase, qaneh ratsuts. For the Assyrian, a crushed reed is something that betrays whoever leans on it. For the servant, it is a weak person he gently protects. Isaiah 30:3–5 and 31:3 make the Rabshakeh's point about Egypt from the prophet's side.

a: It was the LORD who said to me
p: The Assyrian claims the LORD sent him. Isaiah had said as much: Assyria is 'the rod of my anger' (10:5).
b: "Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger! / It is a stick, and my rage is in their hand" (10:5). Isaiah had taught that God was using Assyria to punish Judah, but also that Assyria, boasting in its own strength, would itself be judged (10:12–15). So the Rabshakeh's claim is half true, as the note on 2 Kings 18:25 says. Isaiah's form of the verse has "against this land" twice, where Kings first has "against this place." The answer comes in 37:26: the LORD did plan it, long ago.

a: Don't talk to us in Judean
p: The Rabshakeh scene is almost word for word as in Kings. The differences are small, mostly shorter readings.
b: In 36:3 Isaiah has "went out to him" and lacks the opening words of 2 Kings 18:18, "They called out for the king"; "I say" for "you say" (36:5); no "now" (36:6); "this land" twice (36:10); "to us" and no "son of Hilkiah" (36:11); no "to them" (36:12); "the words of the great king" (36:13); no "from his hand" (36:14); a shorter description of the new land (36:17, see the variant); a differently worded warning (36:18); no Hena and Ivvah (36:19, though they appear in 37:13); and "They stayed silent" without "the people" (36:21). In 36:11 the Great Isaiah Scroll has "these words" and "the men sitting on the wall" (see the variant). On Aramaic and Judean see the note on 2 Kings 18:26.

a: Don't let Hezekiah lead you astray
p: Isaiah's wording, pen-yassit, differs from Kings: 'so that Hezekiah does not lead you astray'.
b: 2 Kings 18:32 has "Don't listen to Hezekiah, for he is leading you astray when he says." Isaiah's form begins with pen, "lest," the verb sut, "to entice, mislead." The same verb is used of the Rabshakeh's own goal of persuading the people. The meaning is the same. Both books then ask the question that the following prayer answers: "Did any of the nations' gods rescue his land?"

a: They stayed silent
p: The king's order not to answer fits Isaiah's call for quiet trust (30:15).
b: Hezekiah's officials obey: no reply, no bargaining. Isaiah had taught that Judah's strength lay in quiet trust (30:15), and he told Ahaz, "Watch yourself, and stay quiet" (7:4). Silence before the mocker leaves the answer to God, which comes in 37:21–35. Kings has "the people stayed silent"; Isaiah has only "they."

a: to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz
p: Here Isaiah is spoken of in the third person, as in chapters 7 and 20. Who wrote these chapters?
b: Most of the book is in Isaiah's own voice, but chapters 7, 20 and 36–39 speak of him as "Isaiah" or "the prophet Isaiah." 2 Chronicles 32:32 says, "The rest of Hezekiah's story, and his acts of loyal love, are written in the vision of the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz, in the scroll of the kings of Judah and Israel." Traditional readers take this as Isaiah's own record, or one written by his disciples (8:16). Critical scholars usually see a later narrative about the prophet. The note on 2 Kings 19:2 discusses how Isaiah enters Kings.

a: So raise a prayer for the remnant still here
p: 'The remnant' is one of Isaiah's great themes, and 37:31–32 answers this prayer with a promise.
b: Isaiah named a son Shear-jashub, "a remnant will return" (7:3), and wrote, "A remnant will return, Jacob's remnant, to the Mighty God" (10:21). With 46 towns taken, Jerusalem is all that is left (1:8–9). Isaiah's answer picks up the word: "Those who escape, the house of Judah that remains, / will again send roots down" (37:31). The Great Isaiah Scroll adds "the remnant found in this city" at the end of 37:4, a fuller form of the phrase.

a: When he heard it, he sent messengers
p: Isaiah says 'he heard' where Kings has 'he again sent'. The two words look alike in Hebrew.
b: Kings has wayyashov, "he returned, again" ("he again sent messengers"), and Isaiah has wayyishma', "he heard." The Great Isaiah Scroll has both, "he heard and returned and sent," which looks like a combination of the two forms. On Tirhakah and the dating question, see the note on 2 Kings 19:9.

a: LORD of Armies, God of Israel, seated on the cherubim
p: Isaiah's form of the prayer adds 'of Armies', the title the seraphs sang in Isaiah's vision (6:3).
b: Kings has "LORD, God of Israel" (2 Kings 19:15); Isaiah has "LORD of Armies." This is the title of Isaiah's call: "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Armies. Everything that fills the earth is his glory" (6:3), and Isaiah saw "the King, the LORD of Armies" (6:5). Hezekiah's prayer confesses what Isaiah saw in the temple: the LORD on his throne above the cherubim rules "every kingdom on earth." On the cherubim throne see the note on 2 Kings 19:15.

a: Assyria's kings have turned all the lands and their territory into ruins
p: Isaiah's Hebrew reads 'all the lands and their land'. Kings has 'the nations and their land'.
b: 2 Kings 19:17 has "the nations and their lands," which makes good sense. Isaiah's "all the lands and their land" is awkward, and this translation renders it "all the lands and their territory." Many think Isaiah's text has slipped, perhaps from the influence of "all the lands" in 37:11. The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks "and their land" altogether and reads only "all the lands," which supports the view that Isaiah's text has slipped; the Greek has both phrases (see the variant).

a: you are the LORD, you alone
p: Hezekiah's prayer ends with the confession that the second half of Isaiah will repeat again and again.
b: "I myself, I am the LORD. / There is no one but me who saves" (43:11); "I am the LORD, and there is no one else; / apart from me there is no God" (45:5); "I am God, and there is no one else" (46:9). The contrast between the living God and idols "that human hands had made out of wood and stone" (37:19) is the argument of 40:18–20 and 44:9–20. Isaiah's form ends "that you are the LORD, you alone," where 2 Kings 19:19 has "that you, LORD, are God, and only you" (see the variant).

a: Because you prayed to me
p: Isaiah's Hebrew lacks the verb 'I have heard' found in Kings, so the sentence runs on into 37:22.
b: Kings reads "You prayed to me about Sennacherib king of Assyria. I have heard" (2 Kings 19:20). Isaiah's Hebrew has only "Because (or: what) you prayed to me about Sennacherib," and then "this is the word." This translation joins the two verses as one sentence. The Greek of Isaiah has "I have heard," as in Kings, and many think the word dropped out of the Hebrew of Isaiah. Either way, the poem that follows is God's answer to a prayer.

a: the virgin, Daughter Zion
p: In 1:8 Daughter Zion was a lonely shack in a field. Here, besieged, she laughs at Assyria.
b: The book opened with Zion all but alone: "And Daughter Zion is left over / like a booth among the vines" (1:8). The city is still hemmed in, but the poem pictures her as an untouched young woman who tosses her head at the would-be attacker (see the note on 2 Kings 19:21). The line breaks of 37:22–35 follow those of Kings, where the Hebrew is the same.

a: The Holy One of Israel!
p: The poem ends its first stanza with the name that marks the whole book: the Holy One of Israel.
b: The title appears about 25 times in Isaiah, in both halves of the book, and only a handful of times elsewhere. Its use here, in a poem found also in Kings, is one reason many think the poem came from Isaiah himself or his circle. The note on 2 Kings 19:22 gives the background. In Isaiah, insulting the Holy One brings judgment (5:24; 30:11–14), and he is also Israel's redeemer (41:14; 43:14).

a: I did this long ago
p: God's claim to have planned history 'long ago' is the argument of Isaiah 40–48 against the idols.
b: "From the beginning I announce the end, / and from ancient times what has not yet been done" (46:10). In 41:22 God challenges the idols to "tell us / what will take place"; in 44:7 and 45:21 he alone has announced things "from long ago." Here the claim is about Assyria: its conquests were God's design (10:5–6; 14:24 "Just as I pictured it, it has come to be"). Within the book this poem is a first example of the argument the later chapters make at length. See the note on 2 Kings 19:25.

a: like fresh green grass
p: The grass that withers before it grows tall returns in 40:6–8, where all flesh is grass.
b: "All flesh is grass, / and all its loyal love is like a wildflower. / The grass dries up, the flower wilts" (40:6–7). In 37:27 the grass is the peoples Assyria crushed. In chapter 40 it is every human power, Assyria and Babylon included, and only "our God's word will stand forever" (40:8). The last line here follows Kings; the Great Isaiah Scroll also has "scorched," but "before the east wind" (see the variant).

a: I will put my hook in your nose
p: Assyrian kings boasted of leading captive kings by ropes through the lips; here God does it to Assyria.
b: A stela of Esarhaddon, Sennacherib's son, from Zincirli shows two captive kings with ropes running to rings in their lips, held by the Assyrian king. The image of God leading Assyria home with a hook in its nose and a bridle in its mouth turns Assyria's own custom against it. Ezekiel uses the same picture for Gog (Ezekiel 38:4). Manasseh, Hezekiah's son, is later said to have been taken to Babylon by Assyrian officers "with hooks" (2 Chronicles 33:11). See also the note on 2 Kings 19:28.

a: And this will be your sign
p: Ahaz refused a sign (7:11–12). Hezekiah is given signs without asking, here and in 38:7.
b: "Ask for a sign of your own from the LORD your God," Isaiah told Ahaz, and Ahaz answered, "I won't ask. I won't test the LORD" (7:11–12). Ahaz then got a sign he did not want, Immanuel (7:14). Here the sign is a promise of three years of harvest that confirms the rescue after it happens (see the note on 2 Kings 19:29). In 38:7–8 Hezekiah receives the sign of the shadow. Isaiah's book sets the two kings and their signs side by side.

a: The zeal of the LORD of Armies will make it happen
p: The same line closes the promise of the child-king in 9:7.
b: "There will be no end to the growth of his rule or to its peace, / on David's throne and over his kingdom ... / The zeal of the LORD of Armies will make it happen" (9:7). Here the same words promise that a remnant will go out from Jerusalem. The repeated line ties the rescue of 701 to the hope for David's line. The Great Isaiah Scroll here has "Zion" and "Jerusalem" the other way around. See the note on 2 Kings 19:31.

a: He will not get into this city
p: Several of Isaiah's earlier oracles promised exactly this rescue, and chapter 37 tells it happening.
b: The siege of Jerusalem and its sudden end were foreseen in 29:5–8 (the nations vanish like a dream in the night), 31:4–5 (the LORD guards Jerusalem like birds over a nest), 31:8 ("Assyria will fall by a sword, not a man's"), 10:33–34 (the forest cut down) and 14:24–27 ("I will shatter Assyria in my own land"). Chapters 36–37 read, within the book, as the fulfillment of these words. Critical scholars often think some of those oracles were shaped in light of the events; traditional readers see prophecy fulfilled. See the note on 2 Kings 19:34 on whether Zion could never fall.

a: The angel of the LORD went out and struck the camp of Assyria
p: Herodotus tells an Egyptian story of Sennacherib's army undone in one night by mice. See also 2 Kings 19:35.
b: In Histories 2.141 Herodotus says that when "Sanacharib, king of the Arabians and Assyrians" marched on Egypt, the priest-king Sethos prayed in the temple and was promised help in a dream. At Pelusium, on Egypt's border, field mice swarmed over the Assyrian camp in the night and gnawed their quivers, bowstrings and shield handles, so the army fled. A stone statue of the king holding a mouse stood in the temple of Hephaestus at Memphis. The story is Egyptian, not Judean, and is set at Egypt's frontier, but it too remembers a sudden, divine defeat of Sennacherib. Isaiah's text lacks Kings' opening "It happened that night" (see the variant).

a: his son Esarhaddon became king in his place
p: Sennacherib was killed by his own sons in 681 BC, twenty years after 701; the book leaps forward to make the point.
b: Babylonian chronicles and Esarhaddon's own inscriptions confirm that Sennacherib was murdered in a revolt by a son, and that Esarhaddon won the throne after fighting his brothers. The details and the names are discussed in the note on 2 Kings 19:37. In Isaiah the scene fulfills 37:7, "I will bring him down by the sword," in "his land," and the irony that 37:19–20 prepared: the king who mocked other gods dies in his own god's house.

a: In those days Hezekiah was sick and dying
t: Why is this story after chapter 37?
p: The illness and the embassy came before the Assyrian crisis ended, but Isaiah, like Kings, tells them after.
b: The promise of rescue from Assyria (38:6) puts the illness before the Assyrian threat ended, but the dates are debated. About 703–701. If Hezekiah's fourteenth year (36:1) was 701, with his accession in 715, the illness falls then and the fifteen added years fill out his 29-year reign (2 Kings 18:2). But Merodach-baladan held Babylon only in 721–710 and for some months in 703, so the embassy (39:1) must be squeezed into 703. About 714–711. Following 2 Kings 18:1, 9–10, others date the accession about 729/727; the fourteenth year, the illness and the embassy then fall in Merodach-baladan's first reign, and some think "fourteenth year" first belonged to the illness story. See the note on 2 Kings 18:13. Either way, Isaiah tells the story after 701 on purpose: many, following Peter Ackroyd, see chapters 36–37 closing the Assyrian age and chapter 39 opening the Babylonian one.

a: I have heard your prayer. I have seen your tears.
p: Isaiah tells the healing in fewer words than Kings, and drops the healing promise and the third day.
b: In Kings (2 Kings 20:4–6) the word comes before Isaiah has left the middle court, God calls Hezekiah "ruler of my people," and promises, "I will heal you. On the third day you will go up to the LORD's house." Isaiah's version has none of this: the word simply comes to Isaiah, and God adds fifteen years. Isaiah also lacks "for my own sake and for David my servant's sake" at the end of 38:6, which the Great Isaiah Scroll does have (see the variant). Without the third-day promise, Hezekiah's question in 38:22 about going up to the LORD's house has nothing to refer back to; see the note there.

a: Here is the sign the LORD gives you
p: In Kings, Hezekiah chooses which way the shadow will move. In Isaiah, God simply gives the sign.
b: 2 Kings 20:8–10 has Hezekiah ask for a sign and then choose between the shadow going forward or back ten steps; he chooses the harder. Isaiah's shorter account has God announce the sign directly. This fits the book's picture: a sign is something the LORD gives (7:14), not something the king bargains over. See the note on 2 Kings 20:9 for the question-or-choice reading in Kings.
orig: וְזֶה־לְּךָ הָאוֹת מֵאֵת יְהוָה (wezeh-lekha ha'ot me'et YHWH)

a: the shadow on the steps
p: What were Ahaz's steps? A stairway used as a sundial, a shadow clock, or a building. See the note on 2 Kings 20:11.
b: The Hebrew uses ma'alot, "steps," five times in one verse. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "the steps of the upper room of Ahaz," linking them to the roof chamber of 2 Kings 23:12. The Greek reads "the steps of the house of your father." No building of Ahaz's has been identified with these steps. Ben Sira remembers the wonder: in Hezekiah's days the sun went backward and he added to the king's life (Sirach 48:23). The chapter page gives the readings on the miracle.

a: A writing of Hezekiah king of Judah
p: Miktav means 'a writing'. Many emend it to miktam, the psalm-title word of Psalms 16 and 56–60.
b: The psalm of 38:10–20 is found only in Isaiah. Its heading is like a psalm title: the author, the occasion. Miktav elsewhere means a document or inscription (Exodus 32:16; 2 Chronicles 21:12). Because the heading looks so much like a psalm title, many scholars read miktam, the obscure word that heads Psalms 16 and 56–60, differing by one letter. The Greek calls it a "prayer," and the Greek Psalter's appendix of biblical songs includes it as the eleventh Ode, "Prayer of Hezekiah." Proverbs 25:1 and 2 Chronicles 29:30 show Hezekiah's court collecting wisdom sayings and temple songs.

a: Halfway through my days
p: Bidmi yamai: 'in the quiet (or the half) of my days'. Hezekiah was about 39, with fifteen years to come.
b: Domi can mean "stillness" or, by a related root, "half." Either way, Hezekiah feels cut off in mid-life. He became king at 25 and reigned 29 years (2 Kings 18:2), so if he fell ill in his fourteenth year he was about 39. The Latin of Jerome, in dimidio dierum meorum, "in the half of my days," is the line that opens this canticle in the Roman Liturgy of the Hours, and Psalm 102:24 voices the same fear: "do not take me away / when my days are only half done."

a: the gates of Sheol
p: Sheol, the world of the dead, is pictured as a city with gates. Jesus speaks of 'the gates of Hades' in Matthew 16:18.
b: Ancient peoples pictured the underworld as a walled city entered through gates (Job 38:17; Psalm 9:13). Hezekiah feels himself being marched off through them. The Greek translates Sheol as Hades, here as "the gates of Hades," the very phrase of Matthew 16:18: "on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not be stronger than it." In Hezekiah's psalm Sheol is the place where life and praise stop (38:18). See the topic page on Sheol.

a: Yah in the land of the living
p: Yah is the short form of the divine name, as in Hallelu-yah. Here it is doubled.
b: This site keeps Yah as Yah, as in 12:2 ("For my strength and my song is Yah, the LORD") and the Psalms. To "see" the LORD in the land of the living means to worship at his house, the hope of Psalm 27:13 ("If I had not trusted that I would see the LORD's goodness / in the land of the living...") and Psalm 116:9. The Great Isaiah Scroll writes "Yah" only once. For Hezekiah, death would end that. Psalm 115:17 says the same: "The dead do not praise Yah."

a: where everything stops
p: Hebrew chedel, 'cessation', is often corrected to cheled, 'the world', by swapping two letters.
b: As written, the line says Hezekiah will be "with the inhabitants of cessation," the dead in the place where everything stops. Many scholars, with a few medieval Hebrew manuscripts, read cheled, "the world, this lifetime" (Psalm 49:1), so "I will look on human beings no more / with the inhabitants of the world." The letters are the same, in another order. This translation keeps the written form, which fits the psalm's picture of Sheol.

a: like a herder's tent
p: Two pictures of life cut short: a herder's tent pulled up overnight, and a weaver cutting cloth from the loom.
b: A nomad's tent can be taken down in an hour and leaves no trace; Zion, by contrast, is "a tent no one will pack up" (33:20). The weaver rolls up the finished cloth and cuts the warp threads that held it to the loom (the word dallah means the loose threads of the warp). Job uses a weaver's picture for the speed of life: "My days fly by faster than a weaver's shuttle" (Job 7:6). "From dawn to dark" means "within a single day"; the line repeats as a refrain in 38:13.

a: like a lion he breaks all my bones
p: Hezekiah speaks of his illness as God's own attack, as Job and the psalmists do.
b: Hebrew poetry did not hesitate to say that suffering came from God. Hezekiah calls God a lion breaking his bones, as Job says to God, "you track me down like a lion" (Job 10:16) and Lamentations 3:10 pictures God as a bear or lion in hiding. Isaiah 31:4 used the lion for the LORD's grip on Zion. The same God who strikes is the one Hezekiah pleads with. The opening words, "I composed myself" (shivviti), are uncertain; some read "I cried out."
orig: כַּאֲרִי כֵּן יְשַׁבֵּר כָּל־עַצְמוֹתָי (ka'ari ken yeshabber kol-'atsmotay)

a: I twitter like a swift, like a crane
p: The sick man's weak voice is like chirping birds and a cooing dove.
b: Sus and 'agur are usually taken as swift (or swallow) and crane; Jeremiah 8:7 names them as migrating birds. The thin, broken sounds picture a sick man who can only whimper, and the dove's "moaning" (hagah) is the same verb used for murmured prayer and lament (59:11). Isaiah 29:4 pictures ghostly voices that "chirp" from the ground. The eyes "gazing on high" turn to God, who is the only hope.

a: put up the bond for me
p: 'Arveni: 'be my guarantor'. Hezekiah asks God to stand surety for him against death.
b: 'Arav means to pledge yourself for another's debt, like Judah for Benjamin: "I will be his guarantor; you can demand him from my hand" (Genesis 43:9). Job asks the same of God: "Please set down a deposit; stand bail for me with yourself" (Job 17:3). Hezekiah feels death has come to collect him, and asks God to stand between them as his surety. Christian readers have linked the image to Hebrews 7:22, where Jesus is the "guarantor" (engyos) of a better covenant.

a: Softly I will walk through all my years
p: 'Eddaddeh is a rare verb, 'walk slowly', used of processions in Psalm 42:4. The verse is hard.
b: The same verb appears in Psalm 42:4, where the psalmist remembers how he would "lead them slowly up to the house of God." Here Hezekiah either vows to walk humbly all his days, or says he will walk the rest of his years with the memory of his bitterness. Some take the line as despair ("I wander all my years"); others as the vow of a man who has been healed. The Greek runs 38:14–15 together and reads quite differently.

a: Lord, on these things people live
t: One of the Bible's hardest verses
p: The Hebrew of 38:16 is very obscure, and translations guess at it.
b: Word for word it reads: "Lord, on them they live, and for all in them the life of my spirit, and you restore me and make me live." "Them" may mean God's words and deeds (38:15), or the bitter experiences that teach. The KJV has "by these things men live"; Jerome's Latin reads "if this is how one lives." Many modern scholars think the text is damaged and offer emendations. The last line is clear: a plea to be made well and kept alive. Deuteronomy 8:3 says that people live by every word from the LORD's mouth, a thought some readers see here.

a: you have flung behind your back
p: Hezekiah's healing comes with forgiveness: God throws his sins behind his back, out of sight.
b: To put something "behind your back" is to refuse to look at it again (1 Kings 14:9; Nehemiah 9:26). Micah 7:19 says God will throw all sins into the depths of the sea, and Psalm 103:12 says: "As distant as the sunrise is from the sunset, / that is how far he has put our rebellions from us." The healing and the forgiving belong together, as 33:24 promised: "And no one living there will say, 'I am sick.'"

a: the bitter, bitter pain I had was for my good
t: For peace, or instead of peace?
p: The first line of 38:17 can mean the bitterness was for Hezekiah's good, or that he had bitterness instead of peace.
b: Word for word the Hebrew reads: "Look, for peace, bitter to me, bitter." Leshalom can mean "for (my) well-being," so that the suffering served his good, as this translation takes it, and as many readers understand the turn of the psalm. It can also mean "in place of peace," as the KJV has it, "for peace I had great bitterness": he expected well-being and got bitterness. The doubled mar, "bitter," stresses how bitter it was.
