The rest of the verse shows that, either way, the bitterness ended in rescue and forgiveness.
orig: הִנֵּה לְשָׁלוֹם מַר־לִי מָר (hinneh leshalom mar-li mar)

a: You loved my life away from the pit of nothing
p: Chashaqta means 'you loved, you were attached to'. Many emend it to chasakhta, 'you held back'.
b: Chashaq is a strong word for love and attachment, used of God choosing Israel (Deuteronomy 7:7). "You loved my life away from the pit" is a bold, compressed line: God's love pulled Hezekiah out of death's reach. Because the phrase is unusual, many scholars read chasakhta, "you held back (my life) from the pit," a one-letter change that matches Job 33:18 and Psalm 78:50. The Greek has "you chose my soul, that it should not perish." This translation keeps the Hebrew as written. Shachat beli, "the pit of nothing," is the grave as the place where all comes to nothing.
orig: חָשַׁקְתָּ נַפְשִׁי מִשַּׁחַת בְּלִי (chashaqta nafshi mishachat beli)

a: It is not Sheol that thanks you
p: Like several psalms, Hezekiah says the dead cannot praise God. What does this say about life after death?
b: "For among the dead no one calls you to mind. / In Sheol, who gives you thanks?" (Psalm 6:5); see also Psalm 30:9, Psalm 88:10–11 and Psalm 115:17. Many scholars read such lines as showing that most of the Hebrew Bible had no clear hope beyond death; that hope came later (26:19; Daniel 12:2). Christians who teach conditional immortality, such as Seventh-day Adventists, take them as plain teaching that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. Catholic, Orthodox, Reformed and most other churches read them as the cry of a sufferer who sees only the end of earthly life and worship, before the fuller revelation of the gospel. The chapter page sets these views side by side.
r: Psalm 6:5; Psalm 30:9; Psalm 88:10–12; Psalm 115:17; 26:19; Daniel 12:2; Ecclesiastes 9:10

a: A father makes your faithfulness known
p: Hezekiah's added years gave him a son: Manasseh, the worst of Judah's kings, was born during them.
b: Manasseh was twelve when he became king (2 Kings 21:1), so, if there was no co-regency, he was born in the third of Hezekiah's added years. The Talmud (Berakhot 10a) tells that Isaiah's sentence "you are about to die. You will not live" (38:1) meant death in this world and loss of the world to come, because Hezekiah had not had children; he answered that he had foreseen wicked children. Isaiah told him it was not his business to know God's secrets. Many readers have found a sad irony in this verse: the father vows to teach his children God's faithfulness, and his son undoes his reform (2 Kings 21:1–9).

a: So we will play my songs on the strings
p: The psalm ends in the temple with stringed instruments. Hezekiah had restored the Levite musicians.
b: 2 Chronicles 29:25 says Hezekiah "stationed the Levites in the LORD's house with cymbals, harps and lyres, by the command of David," and 29:30 that they sang "with the words of David and of Asaph the visionary." The "we" suggests the song was used in worship by others, not only by Hezekiah. Neginot, "stringed music," appears in several psalm titles (Psalm 4:0). In the Great Isaiah Scroll this verse is disturbed: the first copyist repeated words from 38:19–20a, and a later hand added the rest.

a: Let them take a lump of pressed figs
p: In Isaiah the fig poultice and Hezekiah's question come after the psalm, out of order. Were they added, or once lost?
b: In Kings the figs and the question come before the sign (2 Kings 20:7–8). In Isaiah they follow the psalm, where they read like an afterthought, and the question in 38:22 refers back to a promise of going up to the LORD's house that Isaiah's version lacks (see the note on 38:5). Two questions are involved. Were the verses added to Isaiah's story? Many think so, perhaps from Kings, and some translations (the NAB, the REB) move them after 38:6. Does the Great Isaiah Scroll show Isaiah before the addition? Its first copyist lacked both verses, and another hand added them, partly in the margin. Some take that as an earlier text (see the note on 2 Kings 20:8). Jacob Stromberg argues that the scroll more likely shows an omission. A common explanation is that the copyist's eye jumped from "the LORD's house" ending 38:20 to the same words ending 38:22.

a: What is the sign that I will go up to the LORD's house?
t: Going up to the LORD's house
p: Hezekiah's psalm ends 'at the LORD's house', and his last question asks for a sign that he will go up there.
b: The chapter's last words bring Hezekiah back to the temple where he spread out Sennacherib's letter (37:14) and where his psalm promised to play songs (38:20). In Kings the question asks whether he will be healed and go up "on the third day" (2 Kings 20:8). In Isaiah the question stands on its own: the sign he has already been given (38:7–8) is the answer. The Greek of Isaiah turns the line into a statement, "This is the sign to Hezekiah that I will go up to the house of God."

a: Merodach-baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon
p: Marduk-apla-iddina II, Assyria's great Babylonian rebel (see 2 Kings 20:12). Isaiah's spelling is the closer one.
b: Kings writes "Berodach-baladan," Isaiah "Merodach-baladan," which is closer to the Babylonian name Marduk-apla-iddina, "Marduk has given an heir." He ruled Babylon in 721–710 BC and again briefly in 703. Isaiah had already announced Babylon's fall ("Fallen! Fallen is Babylon!" 21:9), perhaps to one of Assyria's sieges in Merodach-baladan's time, though many date that oracle to 539 BC (see the note on 21:9). Isaiah adds "and had gotten well" (Hebrew wayyechezaq), where Kings has only that he had been sick. 2 Chronicles 32:31 says the envoys came "to ask about the sign that had happened in the land."

a: Hezekiah was glad to see them
p: Isaiah has 'he was glad' where Kings has 'he listened to them'. Both books leave the fault unstated; see 2 Kings 20:13.
b: The difference is one letter in Hebrew: Isaiah's wayyismach, "he rejoiced," and Kings' wayyishma', "he listened" (see the variant). Readers have found the sin in pride (2 Chronicles 32:25: "his heart rose up high"), in trust in a foreign alliance, the very thing Isaiah attacked in 30:1–7 and 31:1, or in showing off God's gifts as his own. 2 Chronicles 32:31 adds that God left him "to test him and to know all that was in his heart." Within Isaiah, his treasure contrasts with 33:6: "The fear of the LORD is his treasure."

a: From a land far away
p: Hezekiah boasts that his guests came from afar. In Isaiah, the far land is where judgment comes from.
b: In 13:5 the armies against Babylon come "from a land far away, / from the edge of the sky." In 5:26 God whistles for a nation "from far away" to punish Judah. The Gibeonites tricked Joshua by claiming to come "from a far country" (Joshua 9:6, 9). Hezekiah takes distance as honor; Isaiah hears a warning, and 39:6 names the place to which everything will be carried.

a: will be hauled away to Babylon
p: Isaiah's last words to Hezekiah name Babylon. The next chapter opens with comfort for a people whose time is served.
b: The prophecy, fulfilled in 597 and 586 BC (2 Kings 24:13; 25:13–17), is the first time in the book that Babylon is named as the power that will take Judah. The very next words of the book are: "Comfort, comfort my people, / your God says" (40:1), spoken to a Jerusalem whose "term of service is over" (40:2). Critical view. Most scholars see the Babylonian chapters 40–55 as the work of a later prophet, joined here on purpose, with chapter 39 as a bridge. Traditional view. Those who hold one Isaiah see the prophet looking ahead to the exile he has just foretold. Ben Sira, around 180 BC, says that Isaiah, by a mighty spirit, saw what would come at the end and comforted Zion's mourners (Sirach 48:24). See the note on 2 Kings 20:17.

a: They will serve as eunuchs in the Babylonian king's palace
t: Eunuchs in Babylon, and in God's house
p: Hezekiah's descendants will be eunuchs abroad. Isaiah 56 promises eunuchs a name in God's house.
b: Whether sarisim means castrated men or court officials in general is discussed in the note on 2 Kings 20:18. Daniel and his friends, of royal descent, were placed under "the chief of the eunuchs" in Babylon (Daniel 1:3–7). Later Jewish tradition took the verse literally of them (Bavli Sanhedrin 93b). Isaiah later turns to such men with a promise: "in my house and inside my walls / I will set up for them a marker and a name / that is better than sons and daughters" (56:5).

a: For there will be peace and safety in my days
p: Isaiah's Hebrew makes Hezekiah's last words a plain statement; Kings can be read as a question.
b: Kings has halo' 'im, "Is it not good, if...?" (2 Kings 20:19), which can be heard as Hezekiah thinking aloud. Isaiah has ki, "for," making the words a statement; both books have "he went on." "Peace and safety" (shalom we'emet) is literally "peace and truth," stability. Whether Hezekiah speaks in selfish relief or humble acceptance is discussed in the note on 2 Kings 20:19. In Isaiah's book his story ends here; the next voice is God's comfort (40:1).
orig: כִּי יִהְיֶה שָׁלוֹם וֶאֱמֶת בְּיָמָי (ki yihyeh shalom we'emet beyamay)

a: Hezekiah prayed to the LORD
p: Chapter 37 follows 2 Kings 19 almost word for word; these are the small differences in Isaiah's Hebrew.
b: Isaiah has "what the Rabshakeh said" where Kings has "all the words" (37:4); "he heard" for "he again sent" (37:9); "prayed to the LORD. He said" (37:15) for "prayed in the LORD's presence" (2 Kings 19:15); "LORD of Armies" (37:16); "the whole message," adding "whole" (37:17); "all the lands and their territory" (37:18) for "the nations and their lands" (2 Kings 19:17); no "please" and "the LORD, you alone" (37:20); no "I have heard" (37:21); "servants" and "height" (37:24); no "strange" (37:25); "a field" (37:27); and no "It happened that night" (37:36). In the Great Isaiah Scroll, 37:29 also lacks its opening "Since you storm against me," the copyist's eye skipping from the same words at the end of 37:28.

a: Hear the word of the LORD of Armies
p: Chapter 39 follows 2 Kings 20:12–19 closely; these are the small differences in Isaiah's Hebrew.
b: Isaiah has "Merodach" for Kings' "Berodach" and adds "and had gotten well" (39:1; the scroll 4Q56 there reads "for he had heard," as Kings does); "was glad" for "listened to" (39:2), where also "all" moves from Kings' "his whole treasure house" to "his whole arsenal"; "came to me," adding "to me" (39:3); "the LORD of Armies" for "the LORD" (39:5), the same title Isaiah adds at 37:16; and "for there will be peace" for Kings' question (39:8). The English follows each difference, and keeps the Kings Plain wherever the Hebrew is the same.
